title: Quick Take — Veridical Data Science (audiobook)
description: This book is about practicing data science in a way that is genuinely trustworthy. The central argument is that getting useful, reliable results from data requires more than applying algorithms — it requires critical thinking, domain knowledge, and a principled framework for evaluating whether your results hold up. The authors call this veridical, meaning truthful, data science.

title: Ch. 5 — Exploratory Data Analysis
description: Since our eyes and brains are not wired to detect patterns in large tables filled with text and numbers, we almost never communicate data-driven results by simply handing someone the raw data. Instead, we summarize it — using a mean, a table, a chart — so that shape, distance, color, and size can do the work of conveying magnitude and relationship.

title: Ch. 6 — Principal Component Analysis
description: Answering sophisticated domain questions often involves data that is high-dimensional — data containing a large number of variables. A vivid example is biological gene expression data, which quantifies how actively each gene in the genome is being expressed. Since every person has more than 20,000 genes, every person's gene expression profile is itself a vector of more than 20,000 numbers. The question of how to explore relationships and interactions across 20,000 variables at once is not a simple one. Most of the visualization techniques we rely on — histograms, scatterplots — are designed for examining a few variables at a time and break down entirely at this scale. And it is not only visualization that struggles. Many analytic methods, including predictive models, perform poorly or fail outright when there are more variables than observations.

title: Ch. 7 — Clustering
description: In the previous chapter, we used principal component analysis to create simplified representations of our data by summarizing and aggregating the variables — the columns. In this chapter, we shift focus from variables to observations, meaning the rows. Our goal is to identify reasonable clusters of observations, and we will introduce several unsupervised learning algorithms that can help us achieve this.

title: Ch. 8 — An Introduction to Prediction Problems
description: So far in Veridical Data Science, the focus has been on understanding the structure of data — summarizing patterns, reducing dimensions, finding clusters. Part three of the book shifts gears entirely, turning attention to prediction problems, which sit at the heart of both traditional statistics and machine learning.

title: Ch. 9 — Continuous Responses and Least Squares
description: This chapter introduces two algorithms for predicting continuous responses, using the Ames house price prediction project as the running example. The goal of that project is to predict the sale price of houses in Ames, Iowa, for the year 2011. The two algorithms — Least Absolute Deviation and Least Squares — both aim to quantify the linear relationship between a response variable and one or more predictor variables. Before getting into the mechanics of how those lines are computed, it helps to start visually, to build an intuition for what a linear relationship looks like in data.

title: Ch. 10 — Extending the Least Squares Algorithm
description: The previous chapter introduced the idea of fitting a straight line to predict house sale prices in Ames, Iowa, using a single feature: the living area of the house. This chapter builds on that foundation in two directions. First, it shows how to incorporate many predictive features at once into a linear fit. Second, it introduces regularization — a family of techniques that constrain the fit to produce more stable, generalizable predictions. The focus stays on the least-squares algorithm throughout, but nearly everything discussed here applies equally to other linear algorithms.

title: Ch. 11 — Binary Responses and Logistic Regression
description: So far in our exploration of prediction, we have dealt only with continuous response variables — things like house prices that can take any value along a numeric range. But many of the most practically important prediction problems in data science involve a response that takes only one of two possible values: yes or no, purchase or no purchase, disease or no disease. These are called binary responses, and the class that each observation belongs to is its class label. When we build a predictive algorithm for a binary response, we are doing classification — assigning each new observation to one of the two categories. To ground this in something concrete, the chapter introduces a running project: predicting whether a user session on an e-commerce website will end in a purchase.

title: Ch. 12 — Decision Trees and the Random Forest Algorithm
description: The previous chapters introduced algorithms like Least Squares and logistic regression for generating predictions of continuous and binary responses. While these traditional predictive algorithms remain widely used, the modern data science toolbox also typically includes several nonlinear predictive algorithms. The primary example this chapter focuses on is the Random Forest algorithm, which uses decision trees to generate predictions. Other algorithms you are likely to encounter — Support Vector Machines, Kernel Ridge Regression, and Neural Networks — are not covered here, but classic references exist for those who want to explore them further.

title: Ch. 13 — Producing the Final Prediction Results
description: The traditional approach to machine learning involves picking the best-performing algorithm from a competition run on a single, fixed version of the cleaned and preprocessed training data. That is its blind spot: it explores algorithmic choices but ignores the uncertainty that comes from the specific version of the data used for training — all the judgment calls made during cleaning and preprocessing. In the PCS framework, the unit of comparison is not just an algorithm but a predictive fit: the pairing of one algorithm with one particular cleaned and preprocessed training dataset. By generating predictions from many such fits — spanning a range of algorithms and a range of plausible data-preparation choices — the framework surfaces the uncertainty that lives not just in the model but in the data pipeline itself.

title: Ch. 14 — Conclusion
description: Whether you arrived here by skipping ahead or you read every single word of this book, you have now made it to the end. This final chapter brings the book to a close with a recap of its primary themes and takeaway messages.

title: Ch. 1 — An Introduction to Veridical Data Science
description: To practice veridical data science is to practice "truthful" data science. The goal of veridical data science is to answer real-world questions by collecting and critically evaluating relevant empirical, that is, data-driven, evidence using human judgment calls in the context of domain knowledge. If the empirical evidence is deemed sufficiently trustworthy, it is communicated to domain stakeholders, where it can play a role in real-world decision making and updating domain knowledge.

title: Ch. 2 — The Data Science Life Cycle
description: Every data science project progresses through some combination of the following stages of the data science life cycle, or DSLC: one, domain problem formulation and data collection; two, data cleaning, preprocessing, and exploratory data analysis; three, exploration of intrinsic data structures, meaning dimensionality reduction and clustering; four, predictive and/or inferential analysis; five, evaluation of results; and six, communication of results.

title: Ch. 3 — Setting Up Your Data Science Project
description: In this chapter, we will briefly introduce some software principles that will come in handy when it comes to practicing data science. While the technical focus of data science is often on writing code itself, you also need to provide a sensible structure to your data files, analyses, and documentation so your results will be reproducible and your analyses will be as unambiguous as possible.

title: Ch. 4 — Data Preparation
description: Every data science project arises from a real-world question whose answer is believed to lie, in part, within some data that either has been or will be collected. Perhaps your question is: which house should I buy? To answer this question, you might plan to analyze some data containing information on recent housing sales in your city, where, for each house sale, the data might contain information including how large the house is, what kind of condition it is in, when the house was sold, and how much the house sold for. Your eventual decision about which house to buy might then be based on a combination of your analysis of this data and your domain knowledge about houses and the city in which you live, and your preferences, of course.
